content: 1. Individuals identified as susceptible to measles, regardless of their age, should be vaccinated promptly unless there are specific contraindications to vaccination. 2. Public health authorities should implement necessary measures, including the establishment and enforcement of school immunization requirements, to achieve and sustain high levels of immunization coverage. 3. Most states currently mandate proof of measles immunity for children enrolled in daycare centers. 4. Enforcing these immunization requirements has been associated with a reduction in measles incidence rates. Vaccination for College Entry 5. Measles outbreaks continue to occur in environments where young adults are concentrated, such as colleges and universities. 6. Effective measles control in these settings requires thorough evaluation of susceptibility and vaccination of those who are identified as susceptible. 7. It is recommended that colleges and universities require proof of measles immunity as a condition for enrollment. Vaccination for Medical Personnel 8. Healthcare workers are at a higher risk of contracting measles compared to the general population. 9. Medical facilities should ensure that all employees born after 1956 provide proof of measles immunity. 10. Since a significant proportion of healthcare workers who have contracted measles were born before 1957, facilities may also consider requiring proof of immunity for older employees who may be exposed to measles in the workplace. Outbreak Control 11. All suspected cases of measles should be investigated without delay. 12. A single confirmed case of measles in a community constitutes an outbreak. 13. Once an outbreak is identified, preventing further spread depends on the rapid vaccination of susceptible individuals. 14. Control measures should not be postponed while awaiting laboratory confirmation of suspected cases. 15. Documentation of vaccination is considered adequate only if the exact date of vaccination is provided. 16. An effective strategy to terminate school outbreaks and rapidly increase immunization rates is to exclude all children or adolescents from the outbreak area who cannot provide valid evidence of immunity. 17. Students may be readmitted immediately after receiving vaccination. 18. Experience with outbreak control shows that most students excluded due to lack of immunity quickly comply with vaccination requirements and are readmitted to school. 19. Students exempted from measles vaccination for medical, religious, or other reasons should be excluded from the outbreak area until at least two weeks after the rash onset in the last measles case in the area. 20. Although the risk of acquiring measles is generally low, individuals vaccinated at 12–14 months of age have been implicated in sustaining transmission during outbreaks, particularly in junior and senior high schools. 21. While the effectiveness of revaccination in ending outbreaks has not been conclusively demonstrated, revaccination of individuals vaccinated at 12–14 months of age should be considered in outbreak settings, especially in high schools. 22. If revaccination is recommended, local health officials should define a geographic zone of risk and limit revaccination efforts to individuals within this area. 23. Routine revaccination of individuals vaccinated at 12–14 months of age is not recommended in the absence of an outbreak. Importations 24. Imported measles cases remain a significant source of reported measles cases in the United States. 25. While most imported cases result in limited transmission, some have led to large outbreaks. 26. If susceptible individuals are exposed to a measles case on a common carrier, such as an airplane, rapid reporting of the case to state and local health departments is critical. 27. Other state health departments should be notified to identify exposed contacts and initiate surveillance and control measures. Surveillance 28. As the incidence of measles declines in the United States, aggressive surveillance becomes increasingly important. 29. Known or suspected measles cases should be reported immediately to local health departments. 30. Serologic confirmation should be attempted for every suspected measles case that cannot be linked to a confirmed case. 31. Reporting of suspected cases and implementation of outbreak control measures should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory results. 32. Effective surveillance of measles and its complications can identify areas with inadequate protection, define groups requiring special attention, and assess the effectiveness of control measures. 33. Continuous and careful review of adverse events following measles vaccination is essential. 34. All adverse events following vaccination should be evaluated and reported in detail to local and state health officials as well as to the vaccine manufacturer. Laboratory Diagnosis 35. Traditional serologic diagnosis of measles requires a significant rise in antibody titers between acute-phase and convalescent-phase serum specimens. 36. However, a single specimen can be used to detect the presence of immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibody. 37. Proper interpretation of serologic data depends on the timing of specimen collection relative to the onset of rash. 38. This is particularly important for interpreting negative IgM results, as IgM antibody peaks 10 days after rash onset and is usually undetectable 30 days after rash onset. 39. Asymptomatic reinfection with the measles virus can occur in individuals who have previously developed antibodies, either through vaccination or natural infection. 40. Symptomatic reinfections with measles are rare but have been reported.
